extracted.intended_audience: chemical manufacturers, importers, distributors, employers subject to OSHA Hazard Communication Standard (HCS), and compliance officers/consultants
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and compliance criteria for updating Safety Data Sheets (SDSs) and product labels to conform with OSHA's revised Hazard Communication Standard (HCS), including reclassification, appendix language, timing, and cost-estimation assumptions. Targets employers/manufacturers responsible for chemical hazard communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain SDSs and labels accurate and current
rubrics_metrics.description: Producers of affected chemicals have an obligation under the 2012 HCS (continuing in this final rule) to ensure that the information provided in their SDSs and labels is accurate and current (paragraphs (f)(2) and (g)(5)). They are generally required to revise SDSs and labels in accordance with new information regarding hazards that may be associated with their products (paragraphs (f)(11) and (g)(5)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For every affected product that is newly created, reformulated, mixed with new ingredients, modified with new/different additives, or has any changes in ingredient proportions, manufacturers/importers must review available hazard information (paragraph (d)(2)), classify the chemical per applicable hazard criteria (paragraph (d)(1)), and develop corresponding SDSs (paragraph (g)) and labels (paragraph (f)). OSHA is not estimating costs for activities already required; only incremental costs for newly conducted activities are estimated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review available hazard information and classify chemicals
rubrics_metrics.description: Obligation to review available hazard information (paragraph (d)(2)) and to classify the chemical in accordance with applicable hazard criteria (paragraph (d)(1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classification, SDS preparation, and labeling are required for each affected product as described above. OSHA clarifies that this obligation applies to hazards the manufacturer/importer knows or can reasonably anticipate (see summary and explanation for paragraph (d)). This is not intended to require identification/classification of every conceivable downstream hazard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of downstream-hazard classification (clarified paragraph (d)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA clarifies that an upstream supplier or manufacturer is required to identify and classify only those downstream hazards that the manufacturer knows or can reasonably anticipate, not every single downstream hazard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA revised paragraph (d)(1) from the NPRM to clarify scope because many comments compared the proposal to Process Hazard Analyses (PHAs) and assumed an overly broad obligation. The agency concludes that the final language limits obligations to reasonably anticipated/known uses and therefore many commenter cost estimates based on broader interpretations are not representative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phase-in period and use of normal update cycles
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA extended the phase-in period for the revisions so chemical manufacturers/importers can phase in label and SDS revisions in accordance with their normal cycle of change and need not replace existing labels or SDSs immediately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because SDSs and labels are periodically reviewed and updated, OSHA expects affected parties to fold HCS updates into routine updates to avoid duplicate costs (e.g., avoiding immediate replacement of existing labels/SDSs). This rationale underlies OSHA's decision not to count certain costs (e.g., disposal of old labels, printing plate replacement) as incremental to the HCS change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reclassification time-per-SDS unit estimates by establishment size
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA estimates the incremental time for a Health and Safety Specialist to reclassify a chemical (per SDS/electronic file) as about 30 percent of the 2012 FEA estimate: 2.10 hours per SDS for establishments with <100 employees; 1.50 hours per SDS for establishments with 100-499 employees; and 0.90 hours per SDS for establishments with 500 or more employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using a loaded hourly wage of $61.18 for a Health and Safety Specialist, these times translate to unit costs of $128.48 (small), $91.77 (medium), and $55.06 (large) per SDS. Multiplying by affected SDS counts produced an undiscounted one-time cost estimate of $8.2 million for reclassification, annualized at a 7% discount rate over 10 years to ~$1,168,932.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumed 50 percent of electronic SDS/label templates affected in certain NAICS industries
rubrics_metrics.description: In the PEA OSHA applied a 50 percent factor to the overall number of affected SDSs (electronic files) in identified NAICS industries to derive the number of directly affected templates for aerosols, desensitized explosives, or flammable gases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA invited comment on this preliminary 50% projection; commenters argued the number would be larger, but OSHA maintained the 50% factor in the FEA on the grounds the requirement clarifies existing obligations rather than creating new ones. Affected SDS counts were derived from Table VI-5 in the PEA and the 50% multiplier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revisions to appendices C and D require formatting/language updates only
rubrics_metrics.description: Affected establishments must revise electronic templates for SDSs and labels to conform to formatting and language criteria in precautionary statements and other mandatory language specified in Appendices C and D (e.g., updated signal words, hazard statements, pictograms, and precautionary statements for each hazard class and category).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These modifications involve conforming to formatting and language standards and do not require any testing, studies, or research. OSHA expects many firms—especially those engaged in international trade—to already have GHS-compliant language; updates are therefore limited in scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unit time estimates for appendix C/D template revisions by establishment size
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA estimated the time needed to revise electronic templates for labels and SDSs to comply with appendices C and D would be 10% of the 3–7 hour per SDS unit time used in 2012 FEA, yielding 0.7 hours (small), 0.5 hours (medium), and 0.3 hours (large) per SDS (electronic template).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applying loaded labor rates and baseline compliance assumptions yields an estimated total one-time cost of $18.9 million associated with revising SDSs and labels for appendices C and D, annualized at 7% over 10 years to ~$2.7 million. OSHA used the same baseline compliance rates as the 2012 FEA (see next metric).

rubrics_metrics.name: Baseline compliance rates for appendix language adoption
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA's baseline compliance assumptions for affected NAICS industries: 75% baseline compliance for establishments with 500+ employees; 25% for 100–499 employees; 5% for 20–99 employees; and 1% for fewer than 20 employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These baseline rates were carried forward from the 2012 FEA and used to adjust the counted number of SDSs requiring incremental updates when estimating costs for adopting mandatory appendix language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incremental-cost accounting principle
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA estimates compliance costs as incremental costs required to achieve compliance with the final changes (i.e., costs in addition to those already incurred to comply with existing HCS requirements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA does not estimate costs for activities already required by the 2012 HCS. For example, because many SDSs/labels would have been updated even absent the HCS revisions, some expenses (e.g., plate replacement, disposal of labels) are considered part of routine costs and not fully attributable to these HCS updates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Management familiarization and implementation effort
rubrics_metrics.description: All employers covered by the standard must become familiar with the HCS updates; the nature and extent of familiarization varies by business. In the 2012 rule OSHA estimated eight hours per manager for familiarization/implementation in manufacturing, but the current final rule requires less time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA's PEA estimated management familiarization time varies by establishment size and by whether the establishment must take further actions (e.g., revising SDSs/labels or training employees). Table VI-10 (not in this chunk) was used to allocate affected establishments and associated familiarization costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extended compliance schedule for chemical distributors
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA updated the final rule to provide chemical distributors 18 to 36 months (depending on the nature of the chemical compound) following publication of the rule to implement compliance with all modified provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This change responds to stakeholder concerns that some distributors may need more time to update SDSs and labels, hire contractors, or otherwise comply. The extended timeline was used to account for distribution-sector implementation realities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodology and economic assumptions for cost estimation
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA's cost estimation methodology uses incremental unit times, loaded wages for relevant occupations (e.g., Health and Safety Specialist $61.18 loaded hourly), affected-SDS counts derived from industry tables, baseline compliance rates, and a 7% discount rate over a 10-year horizon to annualize one-time costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA derived unit costs by multiplying unit-time estimates by loaded wages, applied affected-template counts per NAICS, summed undiscounted one-time costs (e.g., $6.4M in PEA, later $8.2M in FEA for reclassification), and annualized results using 7%/10-year factors. OSHA invited comment on these assumptions and adjusted time estimates based on public input (e.g., increasing reclassification time from 25% to 30% of prior estimates).

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivation of affected SDS/template counts from NAICS tables
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA derived the number of directly affected electronic files for SDSs and labels by applying the 50% factor to the overall number of affected SDSs (electronic files) shown in Table VI-5 (from the PEA), and reported affected industries accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in NAICS 211130 OSHA used an overall number of affected SDSs of 15,810 and applied the 50% factor to estimate 7,905 directly affected SDS electronic files. These counts feed into time and cost multiplications for unit-cost estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited scope of current revisions relative to 2012 rule
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA emphasizes that the current revisions are significantly more limited in scope than the 2012 HCS final rule, with fewer affected hazard categories and more limited changes, yielding opportunities for scale efficiencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the present rule is narrower, OSHA adjusted unit time estimates downward (relative to 2012) for many activities, but did increase some estimates (e.g., reclassification time increased from 25% to 30% of 2012 hours) in response to stakeholder input.
